text: Drive through the newest subdivisions in Hidalgo County right now and you'll see it: for-sale signs, model homes with the lights on, and finished houses still waiting for buyers.

There are now more homes for sale in the McAllen metro than at any point in thirty-six years, about thirty-four hundred listings in October, up from fewer than a thousand in the fall of twenty twenty-one.
And just as buyers started to come back, mortgage rates turned on them, climbing back above seven percent this fall, the highest since twenty twenty-three.
So is this the buyer's market the Valley has been waiting for, or a warning sign for anyone building or lending here heading into twenty twenty-seven? Let's go through the numbers. This is RGV News.

Start with supply. Housing economists measure it in months of inventory: how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace of sales. Six months is considered balanced. Less than that favors sellers, and more than that favors buyers.
In May twenty twenty-one, at the height of the pandemic boom, the McAllen metro had roughly two months of inventory. Homes drew multiple offers, and buyers were waiving inspections.
Builders responded the way you'd expect, and hundreds of new subdivisions went up across Hidalgo County.
Now the pendulum has swung the other way. By August, the McAllen metro had nearly nine months of inventory, firmly in buyer's-market territory.

One private lender who finances local builders put it bluntly earlier this year. Some new subdivisions in Weslaco, he said, are "ghost towns, completely empty." But the glut hasn't done to prices what most people would expect.
You might expect all that inventory to send prices tumbling. So far, it hasn't. Prices in the Valley aren't crashing; they're slipping.

The median listing price in the McAllen metro peaked at about two hundred eighty thousand dollars in October twenty twenty-three. This October it was two hundred fifty-five thousand, roughly nine percent lower, while the median sale price has held near two forty-five since twenty twenty-three.

What has changed is how long homes sit, and how hard sellers have to work. The typical McAllen listing now spends about seventy-eight days on the market, compared with forty-eight in the fall of twenty twenty-one, and about one in six listings had a price cut in October.

Builders are sweetening deals with rate buy-downs, appliance packages and warranties, and in some cases new homes are now priced below comparable resales. One new three-bedroom on Gumwood Avenue in McAllen, listed at two hundred seventy-five thousand in February, was down to two fifty-nine by August. And then there's the part of the equation nobody in the Valley controls.

Early this year, buyers caught a break. Rates eased over the winter, January closings in McAllen jumped twenty-one percent from a year earlier, and by late February the thirty-year fixed had dipped to five point nine eight percent.
Then inflation came back. Energy prices climbed with the conflict involving Iran, rates followed, and by October the thirty-year fixed was back above seven percent.

Here's what that does to a real budget. On a two-hundred-fifty-five-thousand-dollar home with ten percent down, principal and interest at the February rate comes to about thirteen hundred seventy dollars a month. At today's rate, it's about fifteen hundred seventy, roughly two hundred dollars more every month, before taxes and insurance.
And sales cooled almost immediately. In September, McAllen metro sales were down eight percent from a year earlier. But rates are only half of the affordability problem.

The deeper issue is income. Over the past decade, median home prices in the McAllen metro rose seventy-five percent, while median household income rose sixty-three percent. In Brownsville-Harlingen, prices more than doubled, while incomes rose sixty-seven percent.

The median household in Hidalgo County earns about fifty-six thousand dollars a year. Spend thirty percent of that on housing, the usual rule of thumb, and you get about fourteen hundred a month. At today's rates, principal and interest alone on a median-priced home is already more than that.

Add property taxes and insurance, and the gap gets wider. One Brownsville broker says deals fall apart when buyers see a monthly note near twenty-eight hundred dollars, and a Valley realtor says some owners are now selling because they can't keep up with the property taxes.

Realtors say real demand sits between one hundred fifty and two hundred fifty thousand dollars. But with lots now running fifty to seventy thousand each, builders say a new two-hundred-thousand-dollar house is nearly impossible to pencil out. That's the gap.
And remember, the Valley isn't one housing market. Brownsville-Harlingen has far fewer listings, about fifteen hundred, and roughly six point seven months of inventory, which is close to balanced.
Prices there are higher, though. The median Brownsville-Harlingen listing was two hundred ninety-seven thousand dollars in October, down from a peak of three twenty-one in twenty twenty-two.

And despite SpaceX and LNG hiring nearby, Brownsville-area home sales fell seventeen percent through August, back to twenty-nineteen levels. Thousands of new jobs haven't turned into home sales, at least not yet.

So what should you do before twenty twenty-seven? If you're buying, this is the most leverage Valley buyers have had in years. Nine months of inventory means you can ask for price cuts, closing costs and rate buy-downs.
If you're building, the gap is the opportunity. Townhomes, smaller homes and build-to-rent can reach the one-fifty to two-fifty range that most new single-family homes no longer can.

If you're lending, watch carry costs. Banks are tightening construction loans, and some builders are now paying private lenders around thirteen percent, compared with about eight at a bank. A home that sits for nine months at those rates gets expensive.
On our watch list: weekly mortgage rates, McAllen inventory, and whether Brownsville sales pick up as port and SpaceX payrolls grow.
The Valley isn't crashing. It's resetting, and in a reset, the deals go to whoever does the math first. This is RGV News.
